label: thm:complexity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:complexity}
Let $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}$ be a filtration of length $n$ of cosheaves over a fixed cell complex $K$, and let $N, p, D, M, \tilde{m}$, and $\omega$ be the parameters defined above. Under the queuing rules specified below and constant-time adjacency lookup, the time complexity to build the reduced complex $K^{\Sigma}$ and its dynamically updated matrices under the \texttt{Filtered\_Scythe} algorithm is bounded by $O((n+1)NpMD^\omega+N\tilde m)$. The space complexity required to store the complex and its matrices across all filtration steps is bounded by $O((n+1)N(p+M)D^2)$.
head: environment

label: def:cellular_sheaf
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cellular_sheaf}
(Cellular sheaf) A cellular complex $K$ with the partial order $\leq$ "face of" defines a poset for us. A cellular sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on it is a covariant functor $\mathcal{F}:\left(K,\leq\right)\rightarrow\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont Vect}_{\mathbb{F}}$. That is, the following hold:

(1). For every simplex $\tau\in K$, $\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)$ is a vector space.

(2) For every $\tau\leq\tau'$ in $K$ there is a linear map $\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\leq\tau'\right):\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}\left(\tau'\right)$.

And the category axioms are preserved -

(1) For every $\tau\in K$, $\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\leq\tau\right)$ is the identity map on $\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)$

(2) For every triplet $\tau\leq\tau'\leq\tau''\in K$ it holds - 
\[
\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\leq\tau'\right)\circ\mathcal{F}\left(\tau'\leq\tau''\right)=\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\leq\tau''\right)
\]
head: environment

label: def:cosheaf
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cosheaf}
\textbf{Cosheaf} is the corresponding contravariant functor, which we will denote $\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\geq\tau'\right):\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}\left(\tau'\right)$ ('extension map'). So that it also assigns a vector space to every simplex, and the composition holds in it in the following way - 
\[
\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\geq\tau'\right)\circ\mathcal{F}\left(\tau'\geq\tau''\right)=\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\geq\tau''\right)
\]
head: environment

label: def:morphism
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:morphism}
(Morphism in the category $\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \textbf{Fun}}\left(K^{op},\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont Vect}_{\mathbb{F}}\right)$) In our case, for every $\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}'\in\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \textbf{Fun}}\left(K^{op},\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont Vect}_{\mathbb{F}}\right)$, a morphism $\psi:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}'$ is a family of linear maps defined for every $\tau\in K$, $\psi_{\tau}:\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}'\left(\tau\right)$ such that for every $\tau\geq\sigma$ it holds - $\psi_{\sigma}\circ\mathcal{F}_{\tau\geq\sigma}=\mathcal{F}'_{\tau\geq\sigma}\circ\psi_{\tau}$.
head: environment

label: def:monomorphism
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:monomorphism}
Monomorphism / Injective morphism ('embedding') in the category $\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \textbf{Fun}}\left(K^{op},\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont Vect}_{\mathbb{F}}\right)$ is a morphism where each of its components is a monomorphism. Since the morphisms in the category are families of linear maps, this is equivalent to the fact that for every cell $\tau\in K$, $\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont ker}\left(\phi_{\tau}\right)=\left\{ 0\right\} $.
head: environment

label: def:filtration
title: Definition
head: environment

label: def:chains
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:chains}
(Chains over $K$ with $\mathcal{F}$-coefficients) For every dimension $m\geq 0$, the vector space of $m$-chains of $K$ with $\mathcal{F}$-coefficients is the product -
\[
\boldsymbol{\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont C}}_{m}\left(K;\mathcal{F}\right)=\bigoplus_{\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont dim}\left(\tau\right)=m}\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)
\]
head: environment

label: def:filtered_chain_complex
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:filtered_chain_complex}
(Filtered chain complex) For a filtration $\left\{ \mathcal{F}_{i}\right\} ^{n}_{i=0}$ of a cosheaf $\mathcal{F}$ over a complex $K$, we denote - 
\[
\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)=\left\{ \boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{i}\right)\right\} ^{n}_{i=0}
\]
equipped with the family of injective morphisms $f^{i}_{\bullet}=\left\{ f^{i}_{j}:\boldsymbol{C}_{j}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{i}\right)\hookrightarrow\boldsymbol{C}_{j}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{i+1}\right)\right\} ^{n}_{j=0}$ where every $f^{i}_{j}$ is an injective linear map. Each such map is defined point-wise as a morphism of the cosheaf, meaning for every cell $\tau\in K$, $f^{i}_{j}|_{\tau}=\psi^{i}_{\tau}$ where $\psi^{i}$ is a morphism $\psi^{i}:\mathcal{F}_{i}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}_{i+1}$. Thus, we obtain an embedding - 
\[
f^{i}_{\bullet}:\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{i}\right)\hookrightarrow\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{i+1}\right)
\]
head: environment

label: def:homology_group
title: Definition
head: environment

label: def:compatible_pairing
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:compatible_pairing}
(Cosheaf-compatible and filtration-compatible pairing). For a cell complex $K$, a partial pairing $\Sigma$ is a collection of disjoint pairs such that $\sigma$ is a codimension-one face of $\tau$. The pairing is called acyclic if it does not contain closed paths. An acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$ will be called $\mathcal{F}-\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont compatible}$ if the extension map $\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\geq\sigma\right):\mathcal{F}\left(\tau\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}\left(\sigma\right)$ is an isomorphism for every pair $\left(\sigma\vartriangleleft\tau\right)\in\Sigma$.
head: environment

label: def:filtration_compatible
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:filtration_compatible}
An acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$ will be called $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}-\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont compatible}$ for a cosheaf filtration $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}$, if it is compatible for each step independently. Meaning, if for every $0\leq i\leq n$ and for every pair of cells $\left(\sigma\vartriangleleft\tau\right)\in\Sigma$ it holds that
\[
\mathcal{F}_{i}\left(\tau\geq\sigma\right):\mathcal{F}_{i}\left(\tau\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}_{i}\left(\sigma\right)
\]
is an isomorphism.
head: environment

label: def:critical_cell
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:critical_cell}
(Critical cell on an $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}-c\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont ompatible}$ with an acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$) Given $\Sigma$ an $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}-\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont compatible}$ acyclic partial pairing, a cell $\tau\in K$ such that it does not participate in any pairing in $\Sigma$ will be called a critical cell.
head: environment

label: def:gradient_path
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:gradient_path}
(Path, gradient path) A path of an $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}-\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont compatible}$ acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$ is a finite sequence of disjoint simplices on $K$ satisfying - 
\[
\rho=\left(\sigma_{1}\vartriangleleft\tau_{1}\vartriangleright\sigma_{2}\vartriangleleft\tau_{2}\dots\vartriangleright\sigma_{m}\vartriangleleft\tau_{m}\right)
\]
where $\left(\sigma_{i}\vartriangleleft\tau_{i}\right)\in\Sigma$. Such a path is a gradient path if additionally it holds that $m=1$ or $\sigma_{1}$ is not a face of $\tau_{m}$.
head: environment

label: def:multiplicity
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:multiplicity}
(Multiplicity) For every filtration level $i\in\left\{ 0,\dots,n\right\} $ the multiplicity $M_{i}\left(\rho\right):\mathcal{F}_{i}\left(\sigma_{1}\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{F}_{i}\left(\tau_{m}\right)$ is a linear map defined 
\[
M_{i}\left(\rho\right)=\left(-F_i(\tau_m\geq\sigma_m)^{-1}\right)\circ F_i(\tau_{m-1}\geq\sigma_m)\circ\cdots\circ F_i(\tau_1\geq\sigma_2)\circ\left(-F_i(\tau_1\geq\sigma_1)^{-1}\right)
\]
We emphasize that there is an inverse map here and then a regular map, alternately. For $m=1$, this means $-F_i(\tau_1\geq\sigma_1)^{-1}$.
head: environment

label: def:reduced_boundary
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:reduced_boundary}
(Boundary operator of a reduced complex) We define the boundary operator as a family of boundary maps, where for each level $m$ we define - 
\[
\partial^{\Sigma}_{m}:\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{m}\left(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)\rightarrow\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{m-1}\left(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)
\]
where for every $i$, $\partial^{\Sigma}_{i,m}:\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{m}\left(K;\mathcal{F}_{i}\right)\rightarrow\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{m-1}\left(K;\mathcal{F}_{i}\right)$ is defined point-wise for every pair of cells of consecutive dimensions in $K^{c}$ by - 
\[
\partial^{\Sigma}_{i,m}|_{\sigma,\tau}=F_i(\tau\geq\sigma)+\sum_{\rho\in\Gamma(\tau,\sigma)}F_i(\tau_\ell\geq\sigma)\circ M_i(\rho)\circ F_i(\tau\geq\sigma_1)
\]
where $\Gamma(\tau,\sigma)$ consists of paths $\rho=(\sigma_1\vartriangleleft\tau_1\vartriangleright\cdots\vartriangleleft\tau_\ell)$ with $\sigma_1$ a codimension-one face of $\tau$ and $\sigma$ a codimension-one face of $\tau_\ell$; the direct term is zero unless $\sigma$ is a codimension-one face of $\tau$.
head: environment

label: claim:is_chain
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:is_chain}
This is a chain. Meaning, $\partial^{\Sigma}\circ\partial^{\Sigma}=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will prove by induction on the number of paired pairs in the acyclic pairing $\Sigma$. We will show that the operation of reducing a Morse pair, equivalent to computing the Schur complement of the pairing block, naturally preserves the chain property.

\textbf{Base:} If $\Sigma=\emptyset$, then all simplices are critical, $\mathbf{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}=\mathbf{C}_{\bullet}$, and the boundary operator $\partial^{\Sigma}$ is exactly the original boundary operator satisfying the property.

\textbf{Step}: Let us assume the claim is true for an old pairing $\Sigma_{old}$ (we will denote it for simplicity as $\partial$), and we add a new matched pair $(\sigma\triangleleft\tau)$, where $\dim(\sigma)=p$ and $\dim(\tau)=p+1$. Since $\Sigma$ is $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont -compatible}$, at every filtration stage $\mathcal{F}_{i}\left(\tau\geq\sigma\right)$ remains an iso'.

We decompose the old chain spaces into a direct sum of the new critical cells and the paired cells, at a typical filtration level
\[
\mathbf{C}_{p+1}(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet})=\mathbf{C}^{\Sigma}_{p+1}(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet})\oplus\mathcal{F}(\tau)
\]
\[
\mathbf{C}_{p}(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet})=\mathbf{C}^{\Sigma}_{p}(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet})\oplus\mathcal{F}(\sigma)
\]

With respect to this decomposition (where the critical cells block appears first and the paired cell second), we can represent the original boundary operator $\partial_{p+1}:\mathbf{C}_{p+1}(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet})\to\mathbf{C}_{p}(K;\mathcal{F}_{\bullet})$ as a block matrix
\[
\partial_{p+1}=\begin{pmatrix}D & B\\
C & A
\end{pmatrix}
\]

Where the components are defined by the reduction of the operator to the corresponding sub-spaces:

$\ensuremath{A=\partial|_{\sigma,\,\tau}=F_i\left(\tau\geq\sigma\right)}$ is the invertible block representing the map from $\tau$ to $\sigma$; that is, the isomorphism.

$\ensuremath{B=\partial|_{\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{p}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right),\,\tau}}$ is the column of blocks gathering the maps from $\tau$ to all the lower critical cells.

$\ensuremath{C=\partial|_{\sigma,\,\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{p+1}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}}$ is the row of blocks gathering the maps from all the upper critical cells to $\sigma$.

$\ensuremath{D=\partial|_{\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{p}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right),\,\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{p+1}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}}$ is the sub-matrix gathering the direct boundary maps between the critical cells.

$\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+1}$ is defined as the sum of multiplicities of the gradient paths between the critical cells (Definition \ref{def:reduced_boundary}). In this induction step, the paths are divided into only two types:

Paths of length 1 - transition between critical cells, represented by $D$.

Paths of length 3 - through the new pairing - start from a critical cell in $p+1$, go down to $\sigma$ - the block $C$, go against the direction from the acyclic pairing from $\sigma$ to $\tau$, where this is an isomorphism represented by $-A^{-1}$, and go down again to a critical cell in $p$ (the block $B$). The composition of these maps from right to left gives the expression $-BA^{-1}C$.

Thus, $\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+1}$ is actually defined algebraically as a Schur complement - 
\[
\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+1}=D-BA^{-1}C
\]

Meaning, exactly the remaining operator after zeroing the row of $\sigma$ and the column of $\tau$ in the block matrix.

Since the pairing took place between dimensions $p+1$ and $p$, the rest of the spaces did not change ($\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{C}_{p+2}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)=\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{p+2}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}$ and also $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{C}_{p-1}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)=\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{p-1}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}$). Therefore, the only operator compositions that might be non-zero are those involving the reduced dimension: The transition $p+2\to p+1\to p$, and the transition $p+1\to p\to p-1$. We will check one and the other will be symmetric to it.

The transition $p+2\to p+1\to p$:

The old boundary operator $\partial_{p+2}$ splits into a block column vector with respect to the decomposition of $\boldsymbol{C}_{p+1}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$ - 
\[
\partial_{p+2}=\begin{pmatrix}X\\
Y
\end{pmatrix}
\]

Where the top block represents the image into the critical cells in $p+1$. Therefore, we define the new reduced boundary operator to be: $\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+2}:=X$.

From the induction hypothesis it holds that $\partial_{p+1}\circ\partial_{p+2}=0$. We will multiply the matrices - 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}D & B\\
C & A
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X\\
Y
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}DX+BY\\
CX+AY
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\]

Since $A$ is invertible, from the bottom equation we get $Y=-A^{-1}CX$. We will substitute, 
\[
DX+B\left(-A^{-1}CX\right)=0\implies\left(\underset{{\color{gray}\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+1}}}{\underbrace{D-BA^{-1}C}}\right)\underset{{\color{gray}\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+2}}}{\underbrace{X}}=0
\]
Accordingly we obtained as desired
\[
\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+1}\circ\partial^{\Sigma}_{p+2}=0
\]

The transition $p+1\to p\to p-1$ is completely symmetric, except that here we operate with a block row vector.

As stated for all other dimensions, the operators did not change and therefore vanish directly from the induction hypothesis. Hence the new operator is a valid boundary operator, and the reduced sequence constitutes a chain complex as required.
head: environment

label: thm:chain_homotopy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:chain_homotopy}
(Chain-homotopy equivalence) For every step $i$ in the filtration, the Morse complex $\mathbf{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}(K;\mathcal{F}_{i})$ is chain-homotopy equivalent to the original complex $\mathbf{C}_{\bullet}(K;\mathcal{F}_{i})$. Moreover, the equivalence maps commute with the filtration morphisms, and therefore the persistence module of the Morse complex is isomorphic to the original module
\[
PH^{i\to j}_{k}(\mathbf{C}_{\bullet}(K;\mathcal{F}_{i}))\cong PH^{i\to j}_{k}(\mathbf{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}(K;\mathcal{F}_{i}))
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us look first at the base case where the pairing $\Sigma$ contains a single matched pair $(\sigma\vartriangleleft\tau)$, where $\dim(\sigma)=p$ and $\dim(\tau)=p+1$. We will drop the filtration index $i$ throughout the first part of the proof for readability. We can do this since the pairing is $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont -compatible}$, and therefore the block $A$ is isomorphic for every filtration level.

First, we will construct explicitly the equivalence and homotopy maps using the block matrix representation defined in Claim \ref{claim:is_chain}.

We will define the homotopy operator $\Theta_{k}:\boldsymbol{C}_{k}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)\to\boldsymbol{C}_{k+1}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$ (an operator of degree $+1$ on the original complex) such that it will act as a lift against the boundary direction through the invertible pairing. 
\[
\Theta_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
0 & A^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
And $\Theta_{k}=0$ for every dimension $k\neq p$.

Using $\Theta$ and the original boundary operator $\partial$, we will define the projection operator of the original complex onto itself as $P=Id_{\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}-\partial\Theta-\Theta\partial$. Where in the two affected dimensions, its matrix representation is

In dimension $p$, $\Theta_{p-1}=0$ and therefore $\Theta\partial=0$, so that 
\[
P_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}D & B\\
C & A
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
0 & A^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0 & BA^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
And in dimension $p+1$, $\Theta_{p+1}=0$ and therefore $\partial\Theta=0$:
\[
P_{p+1}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
0 & A^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}D & B\\
C & A
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
A^{-1}C & I
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
-A^{-1}C & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]

From the operator $P$ we will derive our equivalence maps relative to the reduced space:

The projection map $\Pi_{\bullet}:\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)\to\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$ is obtained from restricting the output range of $P$ to the critical space, meaning taking the top block row
\[
\Pi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
\]
The inclusion map $\Psi_{\bullet}:\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)\to\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$ is obtained from restricting the input domain of $P$ to the critical space, taking the left block column
\[
\Psi_{p+1}=\begin{pmatrix}I\\
-A^{-1}C
\end{pmatrix}
\]

For the dimensions that were not affected by the pairing, the maps $\Pi,\Psi$ act as the identity map. To prove that these maps constitute a chain-homotopy equivalence, we must show two properties, presented in the following lemmas.

\begin{lemma} \label{lem:identity_reduced}
(Identity on the reduced complex) The composition $\Pi_{\bullet}\circ\Psi_{\bullet}$ is the exact identity map on the reduced complex $\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We will multiply the matrices of the affected dimensions.

For dimension $p$: $\Pi_{p}\circ\Psi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I\\
0
\end{pmatrix}=I$

For dimension $p+1$: $\Pi_{p+1}\circ\Psi_{p+1}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I\\
-A^{-1}C
\end{pmatrix}=I$
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma} \label{lem:homotopy_original}
(The homotopy connection on the original complex) The composition $\Psi_{\bullet}\circ\Pi_{\bullet}$ is chain-homotopy equivalent to the identity on $\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$ with respect to the original boundary operator $\partial$,
\[
Id_{\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}-\Psi_{\bullet}\circ\Pi_{\bullet}=\partial\circ\Theta+\Theta\circ\partial
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We will calculate the left side:
\[
\Psi_{p}\circ\Pi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I\\
0
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]

So that 
\[
Id_{\boldsymbol{C}_{p}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}-\Psi_{p}\circ\Pi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & BA^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}
\]

We will calculate the right side. The homotopy contribution in dimension $p$ comes from $\partial\circ\Theta$ only:
\[
\partial_{p+1}\Theta_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}D & B\\
C & A
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
0 & A^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & BA^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}
\]

Overall the sides are exactly equal. A symmetric and identical proof holds for dimension $p+1$, where the homotopy contribution comes from $\Theta_{p}\partial_{p+1}$ and produces the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
A^{-1}C & I
\end{pmatrix}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma} \label{lem:generalization_acyclic}
(Generalization to any complex acyclic pairing) There exists a full chain-homotopy equivalence for the reduction of any acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
According to discrete Morse theory \cite{forman1998morse}, every acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$ induces a partial order relation (a directed acyclic graph - $DAG$) on its elements, defined by the direction of the gradient paths. From a basic combinatorial property of finite acyclic graphs, there always exists a minimal element in them - in other words, a matched pair from which no gradient paths leave to other pairs \cite{kozlov2008combinatorial}. We will perform the reduction of the pairs by induction, step by step, according to a topological sort that will give us the minimal elements and upwards.

The requirement of acyclicity of the original pairing ensures that the reduction of a single pair (which updates the blocks $D,B,C$ of the boundary operator in the current step) only merges existing paths, and will never create a new circular gradient path (Self-loop) \cite{kozlov2008combinatorial,skoldberg2006morse}.

Since we reduce the pairs according to the minimal order, pairs that have not yet been reduced are not part of a continuation path for a pair that has already been reduced. Therefore, updating the matrices / row reduction does not change the original values of the pairing maps that have not yet been handled. This fact ensures that the block $A$ of future pairs in the queue remains unchanged ($A=F_i\left(\tau\geq\sigma\right)$), and therefore remains an invertible isomorphism throughout the entire process, which allows the continuation of the reduction.

Since a finite composition of chain-homotopy equivalences is itself a chain-homotopy equivalence \cite{nanda2022tda,munkres1984elements,ghrist2014elementary}, inductive application of Lemmas \ref{lem:identity_reduced} and \ref{lem:homotopy_original} over all the pairs in the pairing concludes after a finite number of steps. This sequence of compositions is well defined, and induces a global chain-homotopy equivalence that maps the entire original complex to the completely reduced complex.
\end{proof}

\textit{End of the proof of the theorem} \textit{(Isomorphism of the persistence modules)}:

We have shown that there exists a chain-homotopy equivalence for every single index step $i$. Now we will prove that it is preserved along the filtration.

Since the pairing was defined as $\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}$-\text{\fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont \fontfamily{cmr}\selectfont compatible}, the blocks $A_{i}$ are isomorphisms for every filtration level $i$. The equivalence maps $\Pi_{i}$ and $\Psi_{i}$ are completely defined by compositions and sums of the boundary operator and of the extension maps $\mathcal{F}_{i}(\tau\geq\sigma)$ and their inverses.

Since the cosheaf $\mathcal{F}$ is a functor, the filtration morphisms (inclusions) $\psi^{i}:\mathcal{F}_{i}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{F}_{i+1}$ are natural transformations. Therefore, the filtration morphisms commute with all the extension and boundary maps defining $\Pi$ and $\Psi$. Algebraically, we get the commutative diagram
\[
\Pi_{i+1}\circ f^{i}_{\bullet}=\tilde{f}^{i}_{\bullet}\circ\Pi_{i}
\]

where $f^{i}$ and $\tilde{f}^{i}$ are the inclusion maps of the original and reduced complex, respectively.

Since the homotopy equivalence commutes with the filtration functor, it is a filtered-chain-equivalence. As shown by \cite{mischaikow2013morse}, this equivalence induces a natural isomorphism on the persistent homology groups across all dimensions and indices. So that the persistence module of the reduced complex is isomorphic to the original module.
head: environment

label: lem:identity_reduced
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:identity_reduced}
(Identity on the reduced complex) The composition $\Pi_{\bullet}\circ\Psi_{\bullet}$ is the exact identity map on the reduced complex $\boldsymbol{C}^{\Sigma}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will multiply the matrices of the affected dimensions.

For dimension $p$: $\Pi_{p}\circ\Psi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I\\
0
\end{pmatrix}=I$

For dimension $p+1$: $\Pi_{p+1}\circ\Psi_{p+1}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I\\
-A^{-1}C
\end{pmatrix}=I$
head: environment

label: lem:homotopy_original
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:homotopy_original}
(The homotopy connection on the original complex) The composition $\Psi_{\bullet}\circ\Pi_{\bullet}$ is chain-homotopy equivalent to the identity on $\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)$ with respect to the original boundary operator $\partial$,
\[
Id_{\boldsymbol{C}_{\bullet}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}-\Psi_{\bullet}\circ\Pi_{\bullet}=\partial\circ\Theta+\Theta\circ\partial
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will calculate the left side:
\[
\Psi_{p}\circ\Pi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I\\
0
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]

So that 
\[
Id_{\boldsymbol{C}_{p}\left(K,\mathcal{F}_{\bullet}\right)}-\Psi_{p}\circ\Pi_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I & 0\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}I & -BA^{-1}\\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & BA^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}
\]

We will calculate the right side. The homotopy contribution in dimension $p$ comes from $\partial\circ\Theta$ only:
\[
\partial_{p+1}\Theta_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}D & B\\
C & A
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
0 & A^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & BA^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}
\]

Overall the sides are exactly equal. A symmetric and identical proof holds for dimension $p+1$, where the homotopy contribution comes from $\Theta_{p}\partial_{p+1}$ and produces the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\
A^{-1}C & I
\end{pmatrix}$.
head: environment

label: lem:generalization_acyclic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:generalization_acyclic}
(Generalization to any complex acyclic pairing) There exists a full chain-homotopy equivalence for the reduction of any acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
According to discrete Morse theory \cite{forman1998morse}, every acyclic partial pairing $\Sigma$ induces a partial order relation (a directed acyclic graph - $DAG$) on its elements, defined by the direction of the gradient paths. From a basic combinatorial property of finite acyclic graphs, there always exists a minimal element in them - in other words, a matched pair from which no gradient paths leave to other pairs \cite{kozlov2008combinatorial}. We will perform the reduction of the pairs by induction, step by step, according to a topological sort that will give us the minimal elements and upwards.

The requirement of acyclicity of the original pairing ensures that the reduction of a single pair (which updates the blocks $D,B,C$ of the boundary operator in the current step) only merges existing paths, and will never create a new circular gradient path (Self-loop) \cite{kozlov2008combinatorial,skoldberg2006morse}.

Since we reduce the pairs according to the minimal order, pairs that have not yet been reduced are not part of a continuation path for a pair that has already been reduced. Therefore, updating the matrices / row reduction does not change the original values of the pairing maps that have not yet been handled. This fact ensures that the block $A$ of future pairs in the queue remains unchanged ($A=F_i\left(\tau\geq\sigma\right)$), and therefore remains an invertible isomorphism throughout the entire process, which allows the continuation of the reduction.

Since a finite composition of chain-homotopy equivalences is itself a chain-homotopy equivalence \cite{nanda2022tda,munkres1984elements,ghrist2014elementary}, inductive application of Lemmas \ref{lem:identity_reduced} and \ref{lem:homotopy_original} over all the pairs in the pairing concludes after a finite number of steps. This sequence of compositions is well defined, and induces a global chain-homotopy equivalence that maps the entire original complex to the completely reduced complex.
